title: Ang 1163–1167: Namdev in Bhairao
tomorrow: if everything you see will pass, what's worth longing for?

lines: A CHILD WITH A CUP OF MILK.
cards: On a lot of fridges there's a drawing held up by a magnet: a parent with seven fingers, a sun with a face, a name spelled wrong in three colors. Nobody frames it for the art.
It stays up because of who made it, and how hard they tried. On ang 1163, the Bhagat Namdev sings about the plainest gift there is, a cup of milk, and a child who won't leave until God drinks it.

teach.b: In paraphrase, the hymn goes like this. Milk in a cup, water in a jug: Namdev milks the brown cow and brings it in.

teach.h: DRINK IT, OR DAD WILL BE ANGRY.
teach.b: Drink the milk, Lord Gobind, drink it and my mind will be at peace. If you don't, my father at home will be angry. That last line is the one that makes people smile.
It's so small, so human: a kid worried about getting in trouble. Then the turn.
In the hymn, the Lord smiles at Namdev, takes the milk and drinks, and Namdev goes home having seen the Lord. Sikh readers take this hymn in more than one way. Some hear a miracle.
Some hear a picture of love that gets answered. Either way, look at what's offered: no gold, no ceremony, nothing anyone would call impressive.
Milk from the family cow, carried by a child who meant it. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Granth keeps the line about the angry father.
A holy book holds onto a kid's fear of getting scolded, because that's part of how the offering was real.
So when what you have to give looks small or a little wrong, the milk is enough, if it's carried like that.

how: Namdev's milk hymn is sung in kirtan and told to Sikh children; in the gurdwara, people bring what they can to the langar, from a sack of flour to an hour of washing dishes.

o: where Namdev begs the Lord to drink his cup of milk
where Kabir calls the Name a wealth he won't knot
where Guru Nanak opens the morning raga

games.q: the milk hymn — tap the pairs.
p: the Bhagat who brings the cup

s: in the hymn, Namdev offers a grand feast
it's a cup of milk from the family cow, set down with a child's plea.
the hymn keeps Namdev's worry that his father will be angry
a small, human line, and the Granth holds onto it.
Sikh readers all take the milk hymn as literal history
some hear a miracle; some hear a picture of love that gets answered.

games.q: your grandmother asks you to cook something for the gurdwara langar. all you can make is plain dal. your cousin says skip it and buy something fancy. what does the milk hymn suggest?
o: make the dal and bring it; plain and meant is enough.
buy the fancy dish; an offering should impress people.
skip it this time and cook when you're better at it.
games.why: Namdev brought milk from the family cow, nothing grander, and in the hymn the Lord smiled and drank it.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and write one plain sentence to someone you love, the way a kid would: no version, no fixing the spelling, no clever line. Then sit with it in your lap while the time runs.
If you'd like, read ang 1163 before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1163. Where Namdev, in Bhairao, begs the Lord to drink a cup of milk, and the Lord smiles and drinks.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: doodh, milk, the offering in Namdev's Bhairao hymn.

carryVoice: Keep the milk: a plain gift, carried by someone who meant it, and the Lord drank it. Day done.
